text: -low-dose warfarin (average daily dose of 2.6 mg) was safe and effective in patients given chemotherapy for metastatic breast cancer. Prophylaxis with low-molecular- weight heparin has been shown to be effective in patients with immobilisation of the leg,42 and in acutely ill medical patients with risk factors for venous thromboembo- lism.43,44 Standard unfractionated heparin prophylaxis, however, had no effect on mortality in patients admitted to hospital with infection.45 A study46 in older medical pa- tients found that fondaparinux may be effective. Although some studies47,48 have shown an increased risk of venous thromboembolism after prolonged travel, the role of prophylaxis is unclear. A systematic review49 suggested that compression stockings were effective in preventing flight-related venous thromboembolism in low- to high- risk patients; compression stockings and low-dose aspirin may be considered, while low-molecular-weight heparin may be needed in those at high risk.8 Other guidelines11,50 make similar recommendations but do not support the use of aspirin. Treatment of venous thromboembolism. Treatment of deep-vein thrombosis3,51,52 aims to prevent the develop- ment of pulmonary embolism, to prevent extension of the thrombus, to reduce the risk of recurrence, and to reduce the long-term complications of chronic venous insuffi- ciency and venous ulceration. Non-pharmacological ther- apy may include bed rest with the foot of the bed raised, limb exercise, and graduated compression stockings.53 These measures may be adequate in patients with small thrombi confined to the calf veins, although this is contro- versial. Heparin and oral anticoagulants are the mainstay of treatment; they prevent further thrombosis while allow- ing natural thrombolytic mechanisms to act on the existing clot. Anticoagulants may be used with non-pharmacologi- cal methods; graduated compression stockings may re- duce the risk of post-phlebitic symptoms in patients re- ceiving anticoagulants,54,55 and are recommended for 2 years.56 Thrombolytics or surgical thrombectomy may sometimes have a role.57 Heparin has an immediate effect whereas oral anticoagu- lants such as warfarin take several days to achieve their full anticoagulant effect. Heparin is therefore used for initial therapy and oral anticoagulants are used for maintenance. Doses of unfractionated heparin and oral anticoagulants must be adjusted according to laboratory monitoring. In the initial treatment of DVT, unfractionated heparin is giv- en intravenously, as a loading dose of 5000 units, and then continuous infusion at a dose of 18 units/kg per hour, ad- justed according to response;9,56 doses are usually in the range of 1000 to 2000 units/hour.
